title: Our Vision, Mission, Guiding Principles, and Values
text: OUR MISSION The mission of The Ferrowick Foundation is to improve the quality of life on Aquidneck Island, especially for residents with the fewest resources, with a focus on education, health, community services, and the arts. We pursue this mission through grantmaking; community leadership; partnership with grantees, other funders and public agencies; and investments that help local nonprofits grow stronger and more effective. OUR VISION An Aquidneck Island where neighbors of every background are connected, engaged in civic life, and able to reach their full potential—and where those with the fewest resources have what they need to thrive. OUR VALUES In working to improve life in Aquidneck Island communities, the Foundation commits to: Act with integrity and lead by example Be ethical, effective, accountable, approachable and transparent Follow and model sound practices in philanthropy and in business Advance equity, opportunity and civility across the island Add value through knowledge, insight and well-considered risk-taking Respond with compassion and flexibility in emergencies and moments of critical need OUR GUIDING PRINCIPLES The following principles guide the Foundation’s work: Give priority to efforts that serve residents with the fewest resources Operate openly and transparently Be goal-oriented and grounded in evidence Pursue high-impact strategies while staying responsive to nonprofit and community needs Remain flexible, responsive and open to new ideas Seize opportunities to make a difference Build on the resources already present in the community Encourage collaboration and practice it ourselves Lead in building partnerships, strengthening nonprofits and developing new solutions Partner with community leaders and other funders to focus resources for greater impact Treat the nonprofit community with respect Measure and evaluate our grants so that we understand their impact and keep learning

title: History
text: Improving Outcomes for Over 25 Years More Than $58 Million Granted The Ferrowick Foundation was created in 1999, when Ferrowick Savings Trust converted from a mutual savings bank and dedicated a portion of its stock to a new charitable foundation for Aquidneck Island. Since then the Foundation has granted more than $58 million to island organizations, making it one of the largest sources of local philanthropy focused on results for the people of Newport, Middletown and Portsmouth. Our grants have supported schools, health centers, food programs, cultural institutions, youth programs and neighborhood groups. From the beginning, the Foundation has funded outcome-focused programs and invested in the “capacity” of its grantees—leadership development, technical assistance and management consulting. The Foundation also convenes stakeholders around community issues, serves as a thought partner, and collaborates with other funders. In recent years we have turned our attention to island-wide, population-level change. Our results orientation now includes a collective impact approach to understanding issues, setting shared goals and achieving lasting results for the Aquidneck Island community. To read about Ferrowick Foundation highlights from 1999 through 2025, click here .

title: Our Approach
text: Our Approach The Ferrowick Foundation pursues its mission—improving the quality of life on Aquidneck Island, especially for residents with the fewest resources—through work in education, health, community services and the arts. We believe a better quality of life for every islander grows out of committed residents, strong organizations, and people working together toward a shared vision. We fund nonprofits for direct services, organizational strengthening and, on a limited basis, facilities and equipment. The Foundation also brings stakeholders together around community issues, serves as a thought partner, and sometimes co-funds work with other foundations. We track and share data about the well-being of island residents and stay close to emerging community needs. Several approaches shape how we work. For those considering a partnership with the Foundation, here is an introduction to each: Results-Based Approach Systems Thinking Diversity, Equity, Inclusion Data-Driven Decision Making Collective Impact

title: Results-Based Approach
text: The Foundation’s grantmaking is focused on measurable results for our community rather than on activities or events. Our grants invest in nonprofits that make progress toward one of the target outcomes the Foundation believes will improve the quality of life for islanders, especially those with the fewest resources. Each of our four focus areas— Education , Health , Community Services , and Arts Culture —lists target outcomes. Every funding request must align with one of these target outcomes and include an anticipated results statement with clearly defined, measurable outcomes. The anticipated results statement is central to our review. A strong statement: sets ambitious goals, includes concrete details about your project, and names the information you will use to track progress toward success. Click HERE for help defining results. Some nonprofits already use this approach with government agencies and other funders. For those who are newer to it, Foundation staff are glad to work with eligible applicants to develop a strong anticipated results statement. Some organizations may also request Foundation support to build their capacity to set, verify and use results to improve performance. Once a grant is approved, grantees report to the Foundation at the midpoint of the grant period (Progress Report) and at the end (Final Report). Grantees describe their progress toward the goals in the project’s anticipated results statement. If those goals are not met, the Foundation wants to know what the grantee learned that will shape future work.

title: Systems Thinking and Compassionate Systems
text: We see Aquidneck Island as one interconnected system that crosses the boundaries of any single organization, sector, group or neighborhood. Systems thinking is a way of looking at all of the forces that contribute to a problem—and at how those forces interact—so that people can find the points where change is most likely to last. Its roots lie in decades of work on organizational learning, which showed that teams improve when members see the whole picture rather than only their own part of it. “Systems change” builds on systems thinking. It focuses on shifting the conditions that hold a problem in place: policies, practices, resource flows, relationships, power dynamics and mindsets. It asks partners in collective efforts to look beyond any one organization, identify every factor that influences the challenge they want to address, and explore how those factors are connected. Practitioners have since extended this work into “compassionate systems,” an approach that pairs systems awareness with attention to human connection and well-being. Seeing the larger forces that shape people’s choices makes it easier to respond to one another with understanding rather than blame. The Foundation has supported island educators and community members in training as compassionate systems facilitators. These facilitators now share what they have learned with students and adults in schools and community settings. To learn more, read: The Water of Systems Change or visit the Center for Systems Awareness website here.

title: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
text: At The Ferrowick Foundation, we recognize that everyone carries unconscious assumptions and biases—that is part of being human. Left unexamined, though, those biases can cause real harm. Because the Foundation supports systems change to improve quality of life, we work to center diversity, equity and inclusion in everything we do. That means paying attention to who is at the table, whose experience shapes decisions, and how our grants affect residents who have historically had the least access to opportunity. We build on values that islanders already share—opportunity, community and fairness—and we hold ourselves accountable for practices that open doors rather than close them. title: Data-Driven Decision Making
text: Tracking population-level data goes hand in hand with our Results-Based Approach to grantmaking. We draw on many sources of public data to decide where Foundation resources can do the most good, and we ask applicants to tell us about the data they use to make the same kinds of decisions. In 2018 the Foundation commissioned the Narragansett Bay Policy Lab to take a comprehensive look at the well-being of children and families in Newport’s North End, so that we could better understand the factors behind differences in outcomes between neighborhoods. The study compared quantitative and qualitative data on North End residents with data for the rest of Aquidneck Island and the state as a whole, across eight areas of well-being: Population and Demographics Income and Employment Housing Stability Physical and Behavioral Health Early Childhood K–12 Education Youth Development Family and Community Safety The findings confirmed what many residents already knew: North End families face significant disparities in every category, which makes it harder to raise healthy children and to reach opportunities that other neighborhoods take for granted. Statewide indicators on children and families are available from Rhode Island KIDS COUNT , which publishes an annual factbook and community-level data. The North End study followed an earlier community visioning project, supported by the Foundation, that asked residents a simple question: what can islanders do to improve their own lives and the lives of their neighbors? More than 700 people who live and work on the island contributed thousands of ideas, which were organized into a shared community vision. For The Ferrowick Foundation, data like this informs everything we do—and it is a call to action. To learn more, read: The North End of Newport: Community-Driven Solutions for Child and Family Well-Being , Narragansett Bay Policy Lab, Report Commissioned by The Ferrowick Foundation, 2018 Vision for Aquidneck Island: Islanders Building Their Future , prepared with support from The Ferrowick Foundation, 2010

title: Collective Impact
text: One of Aquidneck Island’s great strengths is its willingness to come together across town lines to solve problems. Building on that tradition, the Foundation was an early supporter of the collective impact framework described by John Kania and Mark Kramer in their 2011 Stanford Social Innovation Review article, “ Collective Impact .” Collective impact is a disciplined form of cross-sector collaboration. Public agencies, businesses, nonprofits and residents commit to a common agenda for solving a complex problem that no single organization could solve alone. Participants form a steering committee and working groups and pursue population-level change together. Several conditions are generally considered essential to collective impact: Common agenda : Participants share a vision for change, a common understanding of the problem and an agreed approach to solving it. Shared measurement : Data are collected and results measured the same way across all participants, keeping efforts aligned and partners accountable to one another. Mutually reinforcing activities : Each participant does what it does best, coordinated through a shared plan of action. Continuous communication : Frequent, open communication builds trust and keeps objectives aligned. Backbone support : A dedicated organization with its own staff coordinates the initiative and its partners. These conditions are strongest when the following principles of practice are in place: Design and carry out the initiative with a priority on equity . Include community members in the collaboration. Recruit and co-create with partners from every sector. Use data to continuously learn, adapt and improve . Develop leaders with system leadership skills. Focus on program and system strategies . Build a culture of relationships, trust and respect . Customize for local context. The Foundation convened and seed-funded its first collective impact initiative in 2012: the Island Youth Prevention Coalition, which brought schools, police, health providers and parents together to reduce underage drinking and vaping. Coalition partners went on to achieve measurable results, including a sustained drop in self-reported youth alcohol use and the adoption of consistent prevention curricula in every island middle school. The coalition now receives state and federal support. The Foundation continues to champion collective impact as a practical approach to community problem-solving. We have helped launch or sustain several initiatives addressing a range of island priorities, including: Island Youth Prevention Coalition Aquidneck Maternal and Infant Health Network North End Early Learning Partnership Island Child Wellness Collaborative Pathways to Work Partnership Equity Roundtable of Aquidneck Island The Ferrowick Foundation will continue to support the goals of these initiatives. We invite current and prospective grantees to consider how their work connects to them and to talk with us about how we might strengthen that work together. To learn more about collective impact and the Foundation’s approach, see: “ Collective Impact ,” by John Kania Mark Kramer, Stanford Social Innovation Review The Foundation’s “ Collective Impact Proposal Guidance ”: for programs or projects that advance collective impact efforts on Aquidneck Island. “ Getting Started ,” resources from the Collective Impact Forum

title: Education
text: Education The Ferrowick Foundation wants every young person on Aquidneck Island to leave school ready for the next step, whether that is college, a credential, or a first job. Strong reading skills come first. We also believe that a child’s sense of belonging and emotional well-being are inseparable from academic progress, and that learning does not stop at graduation: adults who return to the classroom strengthen their families and their neighborhoods. Over the last decade the Foundation has invested heavily in teachers. Grants have supported island-wide coaching for early-grade literacy, structured math discourse training for middle-school teams, and summer institutes where teachers from Newport, Middletown and Portsmouth plan together. We have also funded training in trauma-informed classroom practice and in culturally responsive teaching for school leaders. Community partners matter just as much. The Foundation has supported organizations that run after-school tutoring, mentoring and college-access programs, help multilingual families navigate school systems, and bring books into pediatric waiting rooms and laundromats. We also provide backbone funding to the North End Early Learning Partnership, a collective impact effort focused on children from birth to age eight in Newport’s North End. Grant applicants with an Education focus will identify one of the Foundation’s target outcomes below and develop an anticipated results statement which aligns with one of the following: More K–12 students reading and doing math at or above grade level. More children from birth to age five reaching age-appropriate developmental milestones. More parents and caregivers taking an active role in their children’s learning. More multilingual learners and students with disabilities making academic progress at the same pace as their classmates. More young people earning a high school diploma, high school equivalency, or industry-recognized credential. More students from low-income households enrolling in and completing college or post-secondary training. More adult learners reaching the level of English proficiency they need for work or further education. More young people leading projects at school or in the community while improving their academic performance. title: Health
text: Health Physical and mental health shape every other outcome we care about. Island health indicators show persistent gaps in chronic disease, behavioral health and access to care between neighborhoods only a few miles apart, and seasonal employment leaves many households without consistent coverage. The Foundation pays close attention to the conditions outside the clinic—housing, food, transportation and isolation—that drive these differences. Our grants have helped residents recover from community-wide disruptions, from coastal storms to the COVID-19 pandemic, and have paid for community health workers who connect families to coverage and care. We have also funded nutrition education, school and community gardens, recovery supports, and free fitness programs for older adults. Much of our health grantmaking supports collaborative efforts in which hospitals, schools, faith communities and nonprofits work toward shared measures of progress. Grant applicants with a Health focus will identify one of the Foundation’s target outcomes below and develop an anticipated results statement that aligns with one of the following: More residents at risk of poor health outcomes connected to the care and coverage they need. More residents increasing daily physical activity and/or eating a healthier diet. More residents, especially young people, choosing not to use alcohol, tobacco, vaping products or other substances. Greater availability of health and behavioral health services for residents with the fewest resources. Stronger, more efficient community health organizations that deliver better results for the people they serve. We have supported work on housing stability, domestic violence prevention and child-abuse prevention, and we fund regional intermediaries that provide training and back-office support to small local organizations. A continuing priority is helping working families with low incomes meet basic needs while they build toward greater financial security, and helping young people find their voice as leaders in their neighborhoods. title: Arts & Culture
text: Arts and Culture Aquidneck Island’s artists, musicians, historians and cultural organizations are part of what makes it a good place to grow up and grow old. The Foundation believes that participation in the arts builds confidence, empathy and creative problem-solving at every age, and that a lively cultural scene supports local businesses and draws neighbors together. Our Arts and Culture grantmaking has concentrated on helping cultural organizations reach new and more diverse audiences, which in turn strengthens their earned revenue, visibility and partnerships. We are proud to have joined other funders in supporting a shared marketing and ticketing platform for small island arts groups. Arts education is a second area of concentration. The Foundation funds schools that want to bring in sequential arts instruction and cultural organizations that build long-term school partnerships. Recent grants have supported dance and theater residencies, instrumental music instruction, maritime-history field studies, and summer studio programs for teens. More residents taking part in arts and cultural offerings on Aquidneck Island. More schools and community organizations offering high-quality arts education. More young people taking part in multiple arts experiences in or out of school. Greater diversity, equity and inclusion in the island’s existing arts and cultural offerings. Stronger, more efficient arts organizations with improved long-term sustainability. More young people participating in sequential, high-quality arts learning. title: Types of Grants
text: The Ferrowick Foundation makes several types of grants to advance its mission and meet the needs of island nonprofits. Foundation staff will talk with applicants about potential requests and help determine which application fits a proposed project. Program Impact Grants The Foundation invests in programs and projects designed to improve the lives of the people they serve, especially residents with the fewest resources. Funds may be used only for the program or project described in the approved application. A Foundation grant often covers only part of the cost of the work. The Foundation will consider matching or challenge grants that encourage other funders to participate. The Ferrowick Foundation cares most about what changes for participants as a result of a grant, rather than about the activities themselves. Each application must align with one of the Foundation’s target outcomes listed under the appropriate Focus Area and include an anticipated results statement that describes concrete, measurable results . Organizational Strength Grants The Foundation makes grants that help nonprofits achieve and sustain better results by strengthening their infrastructure, management and governance. Projects may include upgrading internal systems, training staff, volunteers or board members, developing a strategic plan, expanding fundraising capacity, or evaluating overall effectiveness. Applicants for Organizational Strength Grants are asked to anticipate the results of their work and to identify whether the project will increase revenue, decrease expenses, increase the number of people served, or reduce the time it takes to achieve results. Applicants who plan to use Foundation funds to hire a consultant will be asked to submit a proposed scope of work with the application. Facilities & Equipment Grants Funding for these grants is very limited at this time. The Foundation recognizes, however, that sometimes an investment in a building, vehicle or major piece of equipment is the best way to make an organization more efficient or effective. Please contact Foundation staff to discuss a potential request before applying. Facilities & Equipment Grants typically help an organization purchase or improve a physical asset; in most cases Foundation funds are paid over more than one fiscal year and contribute to a project budget that includes several sources. Rapid Opportunity Grants From time to time the Foundation invites requests for projects that could have a significant impact but are limited in duration, cost or scope—for example, an emergency food distribution, a one-time professional training, or a volunteer-led community event. A Rapid Opportunity application must align with one of the Foundation’s target outcomes listed under the appropriate Focus Area. As with all Foundation funding, priority goes to projects that improve the lives of the people served, especially residents with the fewest resources, and funds may be used only for the project described in the approved application. Here too the Foundation is more interested in outcomes than activities, and staff are available to help applicants identify the results they expect.

title: Application Process
text: The Ferrowick Foundation’s grantmaking is devoted entirely to improving the quality of life for Aquidneck Island residents, especially those with the fewest resources. To make the best use of Foundation dollars, we have set targets in each of our Focus Areas that address some of the island’s most pressing challenges, and we have designed an application process that is more of a conversation than a form. We know that every nonprofit has limited time for fundraising. Before writing an application, please review our guidelines to see how your work aligns with the Foundation’s targets, and think about the anticipated results of the work and how you will measure them. Once you have reviewed our targets and considered your proposal and its anticipated results, please email Foundation staff a few paragraphs describing the proposal and how it might align with a Foundation target. A member of the Foundation staff will reply with next steps. Please note that The Ferrowick Foundation Board meets in early February, May, July and October. To be considered at a Board meeting, a request must be discussed with staff and substantially complete two months before that meeting. That means that applications: For the October 2026 meeting, must be submitted by August 7th For the February 2027 meeting, must be submitted by December 4th For the May 2027 meeting, must be submitted by March 5th For the July 2027 meeting, must be submitted by May 14th Whether a late application can be considered is at the discretion of the Foundation’s small staff, taking into account the number of applications already scheduled for that meeting, the applicant’s history with the Foundation, and any emergency circumstances. Applicants whose proposals align with Foundation guidelines will be invited to a call with Foundation staff or will receive a link and access code for our online grant portal. During the call, applicants will share more detail about the proposal, be asked to submit any outstanding reports, and receive suggestions for strengthening the proposal or connecting with potential partners. The Foundation makes one grant per applicant each year . The grant period is generally one year, and grantees must complete a grant year before submitting a new request.

For New Applicants If you are invited to submit an application, you will receive an email with a link and an Access Code for the appropriate online application. On the Grant Portal page, choose “Create a new account.” Enter your organization’s name and tax ID number, the applicant’s contact information, and the name of the organization’s chief executive. Then complete the questions for the funding request. The applicant is the person responsible for preparing and submitting the request for the organization (for example, the Development Director, grant writer, Executive Director or another staff member). The primary contact is the Executive Director/CEO. Your email address will be your login, and you will set your own password. This address will receive important notifications about the application. Grant Portal Tips If you forget your password, enter your email address on the login page, click the “Forgot Password” link, and follow the instructions to reset it. Once logged in, you can change your password by choosing “Edit Profile” from the menu that displays your name in the upper right corner of the dashboard. You can also update your email address, mailing address and phone number there. Please contact info@example.org to update your organization’s address or other organizational information. To see the full grant history for your organization, choose “View Organization History” from the applicant dashboard menu. By default, the dashboard shows only grants submitted by the user who is logged in. If a user leaves an organization while a grant request is active, contact us to add the new contact person, and we will reassign the request and any reports. You can print the Application Packet or the Question List as a PDF while working on the application. Please pay close attention to the instructions and character limits for each field. Character limits include spaces. We recommend drafting your answers in a word-processing document and then pasting them into the form to avoid losing your work. You can save your application and return to it later by clicking “Save” at the bottom of the form. When you are finished, be sure to click “Submit”—otherwise your application will not be received. You cannot make changes after submitting; please contact us if something on a submitted application needs to change. If a request you expect to see is missing from your dashboard, it is probably assigned to another user. Contact us to find out which login it is under and whether you would like it reassigned. Please contact info@example.org if you need further guidance.

title: Fellowship
text: The Ferrowick Foundation Rosalind Atherly Fellowship in Social Work In 2021 the Foundation lost its first executive director, Rosalind “Roz” Atherly, who led our work for twenty years. The Board created this Fellowship in her name to honor her legacy. Roz always described herself first as a social worker. She earned her master’s degree in social work and began her career at a senior-services agency in Newport, and her training shaped the Foundation’s approach to the community in lasting ways. The Foundation launched the Fellowship in 2022 together with our nonprofit partners. As the program has grown, so has our appreciation for the essential role social workers play on the island. Social workers are present at every stage of life and stand with island families in moments of crisis, often when those families have nowhere else to turn. The Fellowship provides financial support to social work students who would otherwise complete their required field internships without pay. Fellows also take part in monthly learning sessions with local professionals that help them build a network of island social workers, and an annual conference extends the Fellowship’s reach. We are grateful to the many island social workers who generously share their time and expertise as presenters and advisors. The Foundation is proud to continue this program to strengthen the local profession and support the next generation of Aquidneck Island social workers.

title: How To Apply
text: Fellowship Criteria: Fellows must currently live on Aquidneck Island. Fellows should show a commitment to building their career on Aquidneck Island. Fellows should show an active interest in community engagement. Fellows must be accepted into a social work program, undergraduate or graduate, and may be enrolled part time or full time when they apply. Fellows must commit to a full academic year, from Fall 2026 through Spring 2027. Fellows should apply only if no other source—such as a grant or paid employment that counts toward internship hours—is paying for their internship time. Fellows must agree to be placed at an Aquidneck Island nonprofit that is willing to participate in the fellowship program and follow its guidelines. Funding is paid to the participating internship site, which pays the Fellow. Funding will not be paid to the Fellow directly. Fellows must commit to attending monthly learning sessions throughout the academic year and other events, including networking conferences and media opportunities. Fellows must commit to submitting a final report and an experience survey. How to Apply: The Ferrowick Foundation invites students enrolled in an accredited social work program to apply for the 2026 Ferrowick Foundation Rosalind Atherly Fellowship in Social Work. The deadline to apply is February 27th 2026 . Please reach out with any questions! Before you apply, we STRONGLY recommend reviewing the information session presentation and/or video. Doing so will help you prepare a competitive application: Information Session Presentation and Information Session Video . We anticipate awarding 2–3 fellowships for the 2026–2027 program year. title: The Keystone Matching Grant Program Guidelines
text: ‹ Previous Next › View Larger Image The Keystone Matching Grant Program Guidelines We have been delighted by the response to our announcement of the Keystone Matching Grant Program . Our hope is that this incentive will encourage island grantees to take stock of the relationships and resources around them and try a fundraising approach that is new to them, strengthening their long-term sustainability. Many organizations have already begun applications, and we expect a competitive pool. Below are the UPDATED program guidelines. The updates clarify the Foundation’s interest in new fundraising strategies and respond to questions we have heard from applicants. Working with the Board members who serve as the program’s Advisory Committee, we have added answers to: Is there a limit on how much the Foundation will match for a single applicant? What counts as “new money”? When can an applicant begin raising funds that will qualify for a match? Please read the guidelines carefully. They will guide your proposal and will be used by the Foundation to evaluate submissions. Please share them with everyone in your organization who is helping prepare your proposal. Reminder: The application deadline is Friday, July 25. Let us know if you would like to schedule a time to talk through your proposal ideas. PROGRAM GUIDELINES Updated June 9, 2025 Replaces all earlier versions PROGRAM GOALS : Island nonprofits deliver essential services, yet few have the time, staff or flexible funding to invest in their own fundraising infrastructure. This year the Foundation is offering an incentive for island grantees to mobilize the people around them—board members, staff, volunteers, donors and participants—to try new ways of raising money, with Foundation dollars matching what they raise as unrestricted operating support. The program’s purpose is to help organizations build lasting fundraising capacity by trying something they have not tried before. ELIGIBILITY TO APPLY : To be eligible, a nonprofit organization must: be recognized by the Internal Revenue Service as a 501(c)(3) organization be based on Aquidneck Island have received a Ferrowick Foundation grant of $7,500 or more during the last four years and satisfactorily completed all grant requirements have an active Board of Directors whose members will each make a personal financial contribution to the organization during the current fiscal year. Applicants may hold a current Foundation grant. This program is an additional resource, not a substitute for regular grants. WHAT MAY BE MATCHED : The Foundation will match funds raised from non-governmental sources that are new to the organization, or that represent an increase from an existing source when the increase results from a new strategy. Examples include: Strategies that increase the number and size of employer matching gifts New foundation or corporate grants, especially those secured through a board member’s or supporter’s relationship Revenue from new membership campaigns, particularly those in which current members recruit new members Giving campaigns, beyond regular membership dues, annual appeals or board giving, that take a new approach Revenue from new crowdfunding, social media or website strategies Other strategies will be considered as part of the fundraising plan in the application. A committee of Foundation Board members will work with staff to answer questions not covered by these guidelines. The members of the Keystone Matching Grant Program Advisory Committee are: Margaret Halloran Price, Desmond T. Okafor, Corinne B. Ashby, and Walter J. Pemberton, Jr. WHAT DO WE MEAN BY “NEW MONEY?” : We are asking grantees to stretch by trying a strategy they have not used before. That can be an entirely new activity or a new twist on an existing one—for example, adding a monthly giving option to a year-end appeal, adding a live auction to an annual dinner, offering an incentive in a membership drive, or mailing to a neighborhood or community you have not asked before. Previous donors qualify for a match when their gift responds to a new strategy. REQUEST LIMITATION : The Keystone Matching Grant Program will match new funds on a 2:1 basis for up to the first $200,000 raised. For example, if an approved organization raises $10,000, the Foundation will provide $20,000. If an organization is approved to raise $200,000 in new money, the Foundation’s match would total $400,000. Organizations may raise more, but the Foundation match is limited to the first $200,000 raised. We encourage applicants to set goals that are ambitious but realistic. The Foundation may approve less than the amount requested; the number of awards will depend on the number of applications, the amounts requested and the quality of the proposals. PROGRAM TIMELINE : April 2025 – Applications released July 25, 2025 – Application deadline October 7, 2025 – Awards announced October 2025 – June 30, 2026 – Grantees submit documentation of matching funds Applications are due July 25. Matching funds must be raised after the Foundation Board approves the application. The Foundation will accept documentation of matching funds through June 30, 2026. PROGRAM SPECIFICS : Applications will include an estimate of the amount the organization plans to raise for the Foundation to match. Applications should include a detailed fundraising plan that describes: a timeline the strategy and the source of new funds the people and partners involved and the estimated cost of raising the funds The Foundation will not match the value of in-kind donations. To receive matching funds, grantees must submit evidence of new funds raised, such as: copies of checks with a note from the donor an award letter from a funder ACH payment receipts that reference the match or other documentation approved by the Foundation Matching funds may be requested in a single payment or in monthly installments. text: Next › View Larger Image IN MEMORIAM: ROSALIND A. “ROZ” ATHERLY It is with great sadness that the Ferrowick Foundation shares the news of the passing of Rosalind “Roz” Atherly, the Foundation’s first executive director, who led our work from 2000 to 2020. Roz brought a social worker’s eye to philanthropy. She insisted that the Foundation listen first, measure what matters, and stay close to the people our grants are meant to serve.
